name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: A Unified Gateway for Calling and Governing LLM APIs
answer: LiteLLM is an open source AI gateway from BerriAI that lets Python code and a proxy server call over 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It sits between your application and providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure and Vertex AI. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its Python proxy has a documented history of memory and cost incidents, and a Rust rewrite is in early beta, so version pinning matters.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and distributed from the GitHub repository BerriAI/litellm, which the site's facts record as having 60,054 stars, Python as its language, a custom licence, and a last push on 2 October 2026. It is a library and a proxy server rather than a model or a training framework, and it occupies the gateway layer of the AI stack, the point where application code, agents and tools meet the many provider APIs behind them. The official documentation lives at docs.litellm.ai. The project describes itself as the fastest, litest AI gateway, with a Rust core and a Python SDK, and it exposes more than 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format. The site's blog shows the gateway being extended across an Agent Gateway, a Model Gateway and an MCP Gateway, which places it as a control plane for traffic, identity and spend rather than as a place where models are built.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs are routing and normalising calls to providers including Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex AI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, tracking cost, applying guardrails, load balancing and logging. The tutorials show reliability testing across providers, with batch_completion_models_all_responses sending one conversation to every model in parallel and returning only the responses that succeeded, and load_test_model sending concurrent requests to a single model. The blog describes production concerns the gateway is built for, including SSO and SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails. It is strongest where a team needs one endpoint and one policy layer across many providers, and where per-key, per-team, per-agent and per-customer budgets must be enforced. The identity and FinOps post shows agents registered in an Admin UI, callers authenticated through OIDC, verified context forwarded as X-LiteLLM-User-Id and X-LiteLLM-Team-Id, and MCP tool access restricted by group, for example get_payroll_details limited to finance-payroll-access. The site does not claim LiteLLM trains models or serves as a model runtime in its own right.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is the gentler entry point, since the documented examples are ordinary Python calls and the provider differences are hidden behind an OpenAI-style interface. Working with the proxy assumes more: comfort with deployment, containers, Redis, rate limits and authentication, because the incident reports describe failures that only appear under concurrency, provider errors and infrastructure outages. The official site offers tutorials, a blog with incident reports, and reference material for gateways, budgets and MCP authentication, so a beginner can start from code samples, but the material is written for engineers who already understand HTTP services and API keys. The site does not present a structured course, and it does not state formal mathematical prerequisites, because the work here is integration and operations rather than model mathematics.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem is defined by the providers it speaks to, the list in the site's facts naming Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex AI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, and by the protocols it now supports, including the A2A JSON-RPC interface for invoking shared agents and MCP servers for tool access with OAuth2 authorization code flow and PKCE. Documentation is extensive, with 60 pages read on 2 October 2026 covering tutorials, reliability testing, identity, budgets and incident reports. Community support is visible in the repository's 60,054 stars and in the blog's engagement with customer incidents, including a supply chain attack write-up where the project explained that it calls Mistral's API directly over httpx and never imports the compromised mistralai package. The site also documents LiteAdmin, a Slack admin agent built on a connector that lets an agent handle tasks through the gateway's management API.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM serves both ends, but the site is candid that the Python proxy has paid for its flexibility. The blog reports that the Python proxy peaks around 359MB of memory under load, and that the Rust gateway serves about 15x the throughput, 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11x less memory, 359MB to 32MB, cutting per-request overhead from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms. It commits to sub-1ms overhead with a sub-100MB binary, deployed as a single Rust binary, and says the migration aims for a pure Rust server serving 100% of AI traffic with hot paths such as auth and rate limiting in Rust. That rewrite is in early beta, benchmarked against Portkey, Bifrost and the current Python proxy, so teams wanting the performance today are choosing an unfinished path, while teams on the Python proxy get maturity at a memory and latency cost.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts and the site support the claim that LiteLLM is used in production by enterprises, including one running litellm-database:v1.100.0 behind nginx, and by teams routing Claude Code through Amazon Bedrock. The blog treats it as a current standard for gateway work, with an active release cadence, versioned stable, release candidate and dev channels, and a Rust migration underway. It is not presented as a legacy choice. For someone choosing what to learn, the value is in the operational skills the project exercises in public: provider abstraction, caching semantics, budget enforcement, identity propagation and incident response. The site does not publish adoption numbers beyond repository stars and does not name customers, so claims about market share should not be inferred from it.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is a Python project with a Rust core, so it sits naturally beside Python application code, agent frameworks and data tooling, and it is typically deployed as a proxy in front of provider SDKs rather than replacing them. The documented pattern is polyglot in effect: clients speak OpenAI-style or native provider formats, agents speak A2A JSON-RPC, tools speak MCP, and the gateway translates between them while calling upstream APIs over httpx. It is used with Redis for caching and rate limiting, with Kubernetes for deployment, and with identity providers through OIDC. The site shows it alongside Portkey and Bifrost as gateway peers in its own benchmark, and it does not claim to replace orchestration frameworks, vector stores or training libraries.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site's own incident reports are the clearest statement of limits. A Medium severity incident saw kernel OOM kills, one worker reaching 61GB RSS and thousands of 502s when provider retries and an unreachable Redis combined, traced to a one-line change in PR #38133 and fixed in PR #39491, backported to stable/1.100.x only on 9 September. Another Medium incident silently broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock in v1.91.0 and v1.91.1, dropping cache hit rates from roughly 90% to 25-45% and raising spend 2-3x, fixed in v1.91.2. The project states it owns these outcomes. The Rust gateway is early beta, and the site does not say when it will be complete or how the Python proxy will be maintained afterwards. The classifier benchmark is explicitly limited, run on synthetic prompts without independent review, so it does not establish general accuracy. The custom licence is not explained in the material reviewed, and the site does not state support terms or a roadmap beyond the migration.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
